          IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF                         )

          FOR COMMISSION APPROVAL OF ELECTRIC                         )
          SERVICE AGREEMENTS AND PREAPPROVAL                          )

                          Redacted Confidential Testimony Summary of John P. Laws

         Direct Testimony

                 In his Direct Testimony, John Laws first provides his educational qualifications and
         employment history. He explains that the purpose of his testimony is to support the Company’s
         request for relief in this Application by explaining the business arrangement contemplated by the
         special contracts between Alliance Site & Grid, LLC, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Google, LLC
         (“Google”), to serve three new Oklahoma data centers to be built and operated by Google,
         providing an overview of the agreements between Google and OG&E, and discussing the customer
         protections embedded in these agreements.

                 Mr. Laws testified that Google identified certain project sites in the State of Oklahoma for
         the development of three new data centers and has entered into Energy Service Agreements
         (“ESAs”) with OG&E for electric service at each of the sites. He stated that the aggregate contract
         demand across the new Oklahoma data centers reaches approximately                   by 2036, with the
         ability to scale further from that point. He explained that in addition to the ESAs, OG&E and
         Google entered into separate Preliminary Agreements whereby Google will fund one hundred
         percent of the dedicated transmission infrastructure investments necessary to connect each site to
         the grid, and OG&E will contract for a portion of the generation capacity required to serve the
         need identified in the Company’s 2025 IRP through capacity purchase agreements with Google
         that are priced below market rates. He testified that Google and OG&E began negotiations in
         earnest in the first half of 2025, and that the negotiations of the commercial terms were complex
         and took a number of months to reach an agreement in principle, documented in a Memorandum
         of Understanding executed on November 4, 2025. Through the Preliminary Agreements, John
         Laws stated that Google has paid approximately                   to OG&E to date and is expected to
         agree to pay an additional               for a total of approximately               as a Contribution
         in Aid of Construction, ensuring that existing customers will not bear any of the costs for dedicated
         transmission infrastructure necessary to connect the Google sites to the grid.

                 Mr. Laws then testified regarding the key terms of the Energy Service Agreements,
         explaining that there is one ESA for each of the three Google sites and that, other than contractual
         terms specific to each site, the ESAs are substantially the same. He stated that rates for service
         shall be billed pursuant to the Large Power and Light Time of Use tariff at Service Level 1,
         inclusive of the rider for fuel cost adjustment and all other applicable riders and modifications, and
         that if a new large load tariff or pricing schedule is approved by the OCC, Google’s rates for
         service shall be subject to change as appropriate. He explained that the total contract term for each

                                   He further explained that Google will pay a Supplemental Resource
         Administrative Charge of                per megawatt-hour of energy generated by each
         Supplemental Resource on a monthly basis up to the actual measured energy consumption for all
         three sites.

                 Mr. Laws testified extensively regarding the customer protections embedded in the ESAs.
         He explained that Google is required to pay monthly Minimum Charges regardless of energy
         consumed, with the Minimum Billing Demand never being less than                        of the Contract
         Demand corresponding to the monthly billing cycle. He stated that in the event Google elects to
         terminate an ESA early or reduce up to                           of the Maximum Contract Demand,
         Google will prepay                          of the Minimum Charges for the remainder of the Initial
         Contract Term, subject to a                     written notice that cannot be given prior to the end of
         the sixth year of the Initial Term. He testified that the ESAs require Google to provide credit
         support, noting that the initial aggregate value of the Parental Company Guarantees being provided
         by Alphabet Inc. in support of the ESAs is approximately                     . He further stated that
         Google agrees and acknowledges that any potential adverse rate impact to other customer rate
         classes will be analyzed, reviewed, and addressed by the OCC in each general rate case proceeding
         and each annual prudency review proceeding of OG&E’s FCA rider.

                Mr. Laws concluded by testifying that the customer protections in the ESAs are on par with
         what has been proposed or settled in other jurisdictions, working to protect against key risks
         including fair cost allocation, stranded costs, and customer default. He noted that Google’s parent
         company and guarantor, Alphabet Inc., is one of the largest constituents of the S&P 500 stock
         market indices and holds credit ratings from S&P Global Ratings and Moody’s Investors Service
         of AA+ and Aa2, respectively, which significantly reduce the risk of contractual default.
